As someone who has paid for research through direct payment through the PI to the school for that service, I can tell you that the process is pretty heavily vetted for corruption. You can find instances of improper research, intentionally misleading conclusions, and downright fraud. However, that is certainly not the norm regardless of funding sources - many people working on the paper do not even know (or care) about the funding sources.

My business was traffic modeling, vehicular and then adding pedestrian, and we paid a great deal to a pair of schools for high quality research - and, no, we left it open as there was nothing to patent or claim as IP in the research. Our code and algorithms were protected and our internal process was (is, still) a trade secret but, frankly, there's not nearly as much corruption as people seem to think.

Hell, I've submitted my papers and done peer-review for others. We don't care who funds what and an unpublished paper really doesn't carry a lot of weight without having been peer reviewed. (I hold a doctorate in Applied Mathematics from MIT if you are curious as to my biases and why I have them. I also have a masters in Electrical Engineering but that is not really salient.) We, really, do not care. Funding? That's the PI's job. Unless you are the PI or an administrator, and your pay doesn't exactly change because of this, you just do your work. You publish to get published and achieve tenure or fame or just to advance the science for the sake of knowledge.

I am not saying there is no corruption. I am saying there is little corruption. It is pretty heavily moderated and subject to being reviewed by people who are not financially invested. That's why the scientific process is what it is. (Note, I am not a "scientist," I tell the scientists that they are wrong. Math, it's a thing.)
